decisions.mark: states that staleness is THREE distinguishable axes rather than one flag, and names them
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "`freshness.py` names three axes: ... `data` | Database is older than the source ... `code` | The server process loaded its modules before the source changed ... `schema` | Index was stamped by a newer build than this server expects" | WHY: The answer explicitly states staleness is measured on three separate axes (data, code, schema) and distinguishes the fix for each. || QUOTE: "`freshness.py` names three axes: ... | `data` | Database is older than the source | ... | `code` | The server process loaded its modules before the source changed | ... | `schema` | Index was stamped by a newer build than this server expects |" | WHY: The answer says staleness is measured on three separate axes (data, code, schema), each with its own meaning and required action. || QUOTE: "`freshness.py` names three axes:" followed by the table of `data`, `code`, `schema`, each with its own meaning and "Cleared by" action. | WHY: The answer states staleness is three distinct axes (data, code, schema), each needing a different fix, rather than a single flag.

decisions.mark: explains that each axis is cleared by a DIFFERENT action — a rebuild for data, a client restart for code — which is why one flag would not have been enough
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `code` | The server process loaded its modules before the source changed | Restarting the client only. Writes are refused until then. ... `data` | Database is older than the source | Rebuild. Done automatically on query. | WHY: The answer gives per-axis fixes (rebuild vs. client restart), but it never says that this difference is why a single flag would not have been enough. || QUOTE: `code` | The server process loaded its modules before the source changed | Restarting the client only. Writes are refused until then. ... `data` | Database is older than the source | Rebuild. Done automatically on query. | WHY: The answer gives per-axis actions (rebuild, client restart, nothing for schema) but never says that this is why one flag would not have been enough. || QUOTE: `code` | The server process loaded its modules before the source changed | Restarting the client only. Writes are refused until then. ... `data` | Database is older than the source | Rebuild. Done automatically on query. | WHY: The answer gives different clearing actions per axis (rebuild vs client restart), but never says this is why a single flag would not have been enough.

decisions.mark: identifies that the schema axis can be UNRESOLVABLE — when the index is newer than the server, no rebuild clears it, because rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `schema` | Index was stamped by a newer build than this server expects | Nothing the consumer can do. A rebuild re-stamps the same newer version. | WHY: The answer states the schema axis is unresolvable when the index is newer than the server, and that rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version. || QUOTE: `schema` | Index was stamped by a newer build than this server expects | Nothing the consumer can do. A rebuild re-stamps the same newer version. | WHY: The answer states the schema axis occurs when the index is newer than the server and that rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version, so nothing clears it. || QUOTE: `schema` | Index was stamped by a newer build than this server expects | Nothing the consumer can do. A rebuild re-stamps the same newer version. | WHY: The answer states the schema axis occurs when the index is newer than the server and that rebuilding re-stamps the same newer version, so it can't be cleared.

decisions.mark: identifies that the write path REFUSES rather than warning, and that the refusal is placed ahead of the build decision so a force flag cannot override it
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `stale_code_refusal` makes any write path (`build_or_refresh`) refuse rather than build with old logic. `force` does not override it. | WHY: The answer states that the write path refuses rather than builds and that force doesn't override; the placement ahead of the build decision is implied by the force-proof refusal. || QUOTE: `stale_code_refusal` makes any write path (`build_or_refresh`) refuse rather than build with old logic. `force` does not override it. | WHY: The answer states that the write path refuses rather than builds and that `force` cannot override it, which is the mechanism the item asks for. It does not say the refusal sits ahead of the build decision. The "force does not override" claim implies that ordering, so I counted it. || QUOTE: `stale_code_refusal` makes any write path (`build_or_refresh`) refuse rather than build with old logic. `force` does not override it. | WHY: The answer states that the write path refuses instead of building, and that `force` cannot override it.
